motivation: Miyasaka first used organometal halide perovskites as light absorbers in photovoltaic cells (2009). Park and Snaith then showed in 2012 that solid-state perovskite devices work efficiently. Snaith also found that these solution-processed semiconductors have long carrier diffusion lengths and can work in planar thin-film architectures, which makes them ambipolar. Within little more than a decade, power-conversion efficiencies went from 3.8% to above 26% in single-junction cells and to beyond 34% in perovskite–silicon tandems. No other photovoltaic material has advanced this fast. The work opened a new field in semiconductor physics: defect-tolerant, low-temperature-processed crystals with sharp absorption edges, tunable bandgaps and long carrier lifetimes. Perovskite–silicon tandems are now entering commercial production and promise cheaper solar electricity. This is a discovery of great use to humanity in the sense of Nobel's will. It is also fundamental physics, and it has changed optoelectronics, light emission and radiation detection.
